payload.scope: A criterion of control and systems theory made so engineers can test whether a transfer function is positive-real, the passivity certificate that the KYP lemma and passivity-based feedback design consume.

definition.body: The positive-real property is the map systems theory draws over transfer functions: a proper transfer function G(s) is positive-real when Re G(jw) is nonnegative for every real frequency w at which G is defined, its imaginary-axis poles are simple, and their residues are positive; it is strictly positive-real when the real part is positive everywhere on the axis. The property is the category the discipline keeps, not the systems that satisfy it: the line is drawn by the frequency-domain inequality itself, against the neighbouring lines of positive-stability (all poles in the open left half-plane) and of positive-realness restricted to minimum-phase, and the category persists through systems theory texts that teach it as the passivity certificate, the KYP lemma that converts it to a linear matrix inequality in the state-space matrices, and the named check isposreal of the MATLAB System Identification Toolbox. e.g.: the isposreal check of a state-space model in the MATLAB System Identification Toolbox; the positive-realness condition in the KYP lemma of Zhou-Doyle-Glover (1996); the impedance of a lossless LC network, a positive-real function in the classical circuit texts | not: the positive-real lemma (the LMI equivalence that tests it); passivity (the energy-storage property it certifies); minimum-phase (no right-half-plane zeros, a different line) [formal: functio realis positiva | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: griffin-lim-iteration
payload.scope: An iterative algorithm made to reconstruct a time-domain signal from magnitude spectrogram by alternately projecting onto time-domain consistency and magnitude constraints.

definition.body: Griffin-Lim iteration is an iterative phase-retrieval algorithm that reconstructs a time-domain signal from a magnitude spectrogram by alternately projecting onto the set of signals with the given magnitude spectrogram and the set of signals with consistent short-time Fourier transform properties. Each iteration computes the STFT of the current estimate, replaces the magnitude with the target magnitude, applies inverse STFT, and repeats. Parameters: (1) number of iterations; (2) STFT window length and hop size; (3) initialization method. It persists as a standard phase retrieval technique in audio synthesis, implemented in libraries such as librosa.griffinlim and scipy.signal. e.g.: librosa.griffinlim used to reconstruct audio from a magnitude spectrogram in music information retrieval demos; Griffin-Lim iteration in the MIRToolbox for spectrogram inversion; the Griffin-Lim algorithm in the phase retrieval chapter of the DSP textbook by Oppenheim and Schafer | not: phase vocoder (phase manipulation for time stretch, not magnitude-constrained inversion); inverse STFT with known phase (direct reconstruction, not iterative) [formal: iteratio Griffin-Lim | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

definition.body: A Krylov subspace is a nested sequence of vector subspaces constructed from a square matrix A and a starting vector v by successive powers of A applied to v. definition.body: The Arnoldi algorithm constructs an orthonormal basis Q_m for the Krylov subspace K_m(A,v) of an n×n matrix A and starting vector v. payload.name: gerchberg-saxton-algorithm
payload.scope: An iterative phase-recovery procedure made to reconstruct a function when the magnitude is known in two conjugate domains but the phase is lost in both, by alternating projections that enforce each magnitude constraint in turn.

definition.body: The Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm is an iterative projection algorithm that recovers a phase function from two domains where the magnitude constraint is known in each. It alternates between Fourier-transforming between the two domains and replacing the magnitude in each domain with the known constraint while preserving the current phase estimate. Parameters: (1) the two conjugate domains (typically spatial and frequency); (2) the known magnitude functions in each domain; (3) the number of iterations; (4) optional relaxation parameters. payload.name: homomorphic-filter
payload.scope: A signal-processing procedure made to separate multiplicatively or convolutively mixed signal components by transforming into a cepstral domain where multiplication becomes addition, processing separately, and transforming back.

definition.body: The homomorphic filter is a signal-processing procedure that separates mixed components by transforming the signal into a cepstral (homomorphic) domain via: (1) taking the Fourier transform of the signal; (2) computing the logarithm of the complex spectrum; (3) applying the inverse Fourier transform to obtain the cepstral representation. In this domain, convolutive mixing becomes additive, allowing separate filtering of components. The procedure then filters in the cepstral domain, applies the exponential to reverse the log, and computes the inverse Fourier transform to return to the time domain. Parameters: (1) the transformation path (Fourier to log to inverse Fourier); (2) the cepstral region of interest (low-quefrency for slowly varying envelope, high-quefrency for rapid variations); (3) the filter applied in the cepstral domain (e.g., a lifter). It persists as the theoretical foundation of cepstral analysis, implemented in speech recognition front-ends, speaker diarization systems, and audio source separation pipelines. e.g.: SRToolbox homomorphic filter for pitch extraction; librosa.feature.mfcc for cepstral coefficient extraction; MATLAB homomorphic deconvolution examples for speech processing | not: cepstral-domain (the representation space, not the filtering procedure); low-pass filter (a generic filter type, not the homomorphic transformation-based procedure) [formal: filtro homomorphice | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: singular-value-decomposition
payload.scope: A matrix factorization method made to decompose a matrix into orthogonal rotations and a diagonal scaling, enabling rank determination, least-squares solutions, and dimensionality reduction.

definition.body: The singular value decomposition (SVD) is a matrix factorization that expresses any real or complex matrix A of dimensions m×n as the product A = UΣV^T, where U is an m×m orthogonal matrix of left singular vectors, Σ is an m×n diagonal matrix with non-negative singular values in descending order, and V is an n×n orthogonal matrix of right singular vectors. Parameters: (1) the input matrix A; (2) the truncation rank k (optional, for low-rank approximation). The singular values σ_i = sqrt(eigenvalues of A^T·A) uniquely determine the matrix rank, condition number, and spectral norm. It persists as the foundational numerical linear algebra routine in data science, signal processing, and machine learning, implemented in LAPACK (dgesvd), NumPy/SciPy (numpy.linalg.svd), MATLAB (svd function), and distributed linear algebra frameworks (Apache Spark MLlib). e.g.: NumPy linalg.svd function in Python data analysis pipelines; MATLAB svd function in control systems engineering; LAPACK dgesvd routine in scientific computing libraries | not: eigendecomposition (only applies to square matrices, not general rectangular matrices); principal component analysis (a statistical technique that may use SVD as a computational tool) [formal: decompositio valorum singularium | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: minimum-phase
payload.scope: A signal classification made to distinguish systems whose phase response achieves the minimum possible phase delay for a given magnitude response, enabling causal reconstruction of phase from magnitude alone.

definition.body: The minimum-phase property classifies a causal, stable linear time-invariant system whose all zeros lie strictly inside the unit circle (discrete-time) or left half-plane (continuous-time). Equivalently, a system with minimum phase has the minimum possible group delay among all systems sharing its magnitude response. A minimum-phase system's phase can be uniquely recovered from its magnitude response via the Hilbert transform relationship between log-magnitude and phase. Parameters: (1) the system's impulse response or transfer function; (2) the region of convergence constraint (causality and stability). Minimum-phase systems persist as the standard model in audio equalizer design, speech synthesis, and communications channel equalization, implemented in MATLAB's minphase function, audio processing toolboxes for minimum-phase filter design, and speech synthesis pipelines. e.g.: MATLAB minphase function for converting linear-phase FIR to minimum-phase; the minimum-phase filter design in the Speech Synthesis Toolbox for vocoder processing; minimum-phase reconstruction in the librosa.effects.preemphasis module for audio preprocessing | not: maximum-phase (zeros outside unit circle, opposite phase delay behavior); linear-phase (constant group delay, not minimum phase delay) [formal: phase minimus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lattice-filter
payload.scope: Built to implement digital filters with cascaded two-port stages that provide superior numerical stability and simpler coefficient adaptation compared to direct-form structures.

definition.body: A lattice filter is a digital signal processing structure composed of cascaded stages (sections), where each stage implements a two-port network characterized by a reflection coefficient. The structure processes input signals through forward and backward prediction paths, with the reflection coefficients controlling the coupling between stages. Parameters: (1) reflection coefficients, also called coupling or Schur parameters, which determine the filter's frequency response; (2) number of stages (order n), which equals the number of reflection coefficients; (3) input type - raw signal, prediction error, or partial correlation. The architecture implements the same transfer function as an equivalent direct-form IIR or FIR filter but with superior numerical stability and simpler coefficient adaptation, making it the preferred structure for adaptive filtering algorithms (LMS lattice, RLS lattice). payload.name: wiener-deconvolution
payload.scope: Developed as an optimal frequency-domain filter for reversing convolution-based signal degradation in the presence of noise, providing minimum-mean-square-error restoration for blurred images, seismic data, and audio signals.

definition.body: Wiener deconvolution is a signal restoration technique that reverses the effects of convolution-based degradation (such as blur or noise) by applying the optimal Wiener filter in the frequency domain. Given a degraded observation y(n) = h(n) * x(n) + v(n) where h is the known or estimated point-spread function (blur kernel) and v is additive noise, the Wiener filter in the frequency domain is H_wiener(f) = H*(f) / (|H(f)|² + S_v(f)/S_x(f)), where H(f) is the Fourier transform of the blur kernel, S_v(f) is the noise power spectral density, and S_x(f) is the signal power spectral density. The restored signal is obtained by multiplying the Fourier transform of y by H_wiener and taking the inverse Fourier transform. Parameters: blur kernel (h), noise-to-signal power ratio (regularization parameter); it produces a minimum-mean-square-error estimate of the original signal. The persistence mechanism is its widespread use in image processing, astronomy, geophysics, and medical imaging, implemented in libraries like scikit-image and MATLAB's deconvwiener. e.g.: the deconvwiener function in MATLAB for restoring blurred images with known noise levels; the wiener deconvolution step in the Richardson-Lucy image deblurring pipeline for astronomical imaging; the wiener-based audio de-noiser in the librosa library for reverberation reduction; the spectral Wiener deconvolution in seismic data processing for improving vertical resolution of subsurface reflections | not: inverse filter deconvolution (applies 1/H(f) without noise regularization, unstable in presence of noise); Richardson-Lucy deconvolution (iterative maximum-likelihood method for Poisson noise, not minimum-mean-square-error) [formal: Wieneri deconvolutio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: kalman-decomposition
payload.scope: Developed as a canonical state-space partitioning that separates linear systems into controllable and observable subspaces, enabling model reduction, observer design, and structural analysis of dynamic systems.

definition.body: Kalman decomposition is a canonical state-space decomposition technique that partitions the state vector of a linear time-invariant system into four disjoint subspaces: controllable and observable, controllable but unobservable, uncontrollable but observable, and uncontrollable and unobservable. definition.body: The Lanczos algorithm is an iterative method for computing a few eigenvalues and eigenvectors of large sparse symmetric (or Hermitian) matrices. It constructs an orthonormal basis for the Krylov subspace K_m(A,v) of a symmetric matrix A and starting vector v, but exploits symmetry to produce a three-term recurrence instead of the full Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization used by Arnoldi. The algorithm maps A to a real symmetric tridiagonal matrix T_m = Q_m^T A Q_m whose eigenvalues approximate those of A. Parameters: (1) the symmetric matrix A; (2) the starting vector v; (3) the iteration count m < n.
